transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-09
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Jae Park (CTO, Polaris), Simone Alvarez (ML Eng), Ravi Patel (SRE)

--- Auto-generated Summary (may be incomplete) ---
Redwood ran a demo that combined long-context handling and high-throughput streaming. Showed console telemetry, routing fallbacks, and Optimize suggestions. Discussed security (SOC2, KMS) and pilot next steps.

--- Transcript Body ---
[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're gonna walk through an edge playbook for the combined case — long context plus heavy TPS and streaming backpressure. Liam will drive the demo.
[00:00:12] Jae: thanks Maya, excited. To set context, our main use case is session-based product recommendations with full chat history, sometimes 30 to 50k tokens. During flash sales we see spikes to about 1.8k to 2.2k reqs per second for short windows, and we need streaming updates to the frontend.
[00:00:30] Simone: yeah and for us latency p95 needs to be under 300ms for token streaming otherwise frontend UX degrades. We also care about cost — can't afford constant dedicated fleets.
[00:00:45] Liam: got it. quick clarification — when you say 30 to 50k tokens, is that raw tokens or with context compression?
[00:00:52] Simone: raw tokens. We do some summarization but we still send a lot — older sessions retained for personalization.
[00:01:02] Maya: perfect. so we'll show three things: how the runtime behaves on long KV cache and sequence lengths, how batching and prefix caching in Optimize can reduce token cost and improve throughput, and how streaming fallback and graceful timeouts work when backpressure hits.
[00:01:16] Liam: opening the console — ok I'm sharing screen, you'll see the per-route telemetry. This is a synthetic run we prepared that simulates 2k rps bursts and sequences up to 50k tokens. note: synthetic latencies are biased by our generator.
[00:01:34] [00:02:00] Liam: first panel — token breakdown. you can see the token service time going up as context grows, and our kernel selection flips to a long-context optimized path around 32k. sometimes the profiler labels are wrong — it might say "long-kernel-v2" as "long cannel" in the export, FYI.
[00:02:20] Ravi: can you explain the kernel switching? does that require model conversion or is on-the-fly?
[00:02:28] Liam: it's on-the-fly — runtime picks execution kernels based on sequence length distribution and configured quantization profile. for very long sequence lengths we prefer the attention-rewrite path which uses streaming attention blocks. there is a memory-vs-latency tradeoff.
[00:02:45] Simone: do you evict KV cache when it gets to X size? how deterministic is eviction?
[00:02:51] Liam: yes — we have configurable eviction policies. default is LRU by token block; you can pin recent prefixes. we also support partial prefix caching for common system prompts so you don't recompute the first 8k tokens each call.
[00:03:05] Jae: hmm, we really need a strong guarantee about tail latency during the flash windows, even if it costs more. can Redwood route to a cheaper but higher-latency model automatically afterwards?
[00:03:15] Maya: yes — routing policies let you specify primary and fallback model families. you can route by latency SLOs or cost budgets. for example route to the high-capacity low-latency model during the burst and fall back to a cheaper quantized variant when CPU/GPU load crosses threshold.
[00:03:30] [00:04:00] Liam: switching to the Optimize view — this is the suggestion engine. it recommends batching window size, a quantization profile, and whether to enable prefix caching given your seq-length histogram. our suggestion says: use batching up to 32 requests, enable prefix cache for 8k chunks, and use 4-bit q5 for steady-state cost.
[00:04:20] Simone: about batching — if we batch 32 requests, doesn't streaming latency increase because you're waiting to fill the batch?
[00:04:28] Liam: good point. Optimize predicts the tradeoff. for streaming endpoints we recommend hybrid continuous batching: small immediate micro-batches (1–3) for low-latency tails and background accumulation for cost. you can set a max batching delay, e.g., 15ms, so UX doesn't notice.
[00:04:42] Ravi: what happens if the queue backs up? do you shed sessions or degrade quality?
[00:04:48] Liam: there are multiple strategies: prioritized shedding (drop low-priority background tasks), graceful truncation (drop oldest context frames), or model fallbacks. streaming backpressure triggers a per-session TTL and then a fallback which returns partial content with a flag for the frontend to refresh.
[00:05:03] Jae: can you show an example of streaming fallback?
[00:05:06] Liam: sure — I'll trigger a synthetic saturation. watch the stream and the logs.
[00:05:12] [00:05:45] Liam: ok hitting 2k rps now. you'll see some sessions get routed to the fallback pool — the console marks them in orange and a reason code, e.g., "KV_CACHE_MISS + QUEUE_DEPTH". here's an example payload: the stream emitted partial tokens and a final "incomplete:true" field.
[00:05:58] Simone: the partial payload — does the client need to stitch a second call? how is state preserved?
[00:06:03] Liam: the client receives a session id and the runtime stores KV fragments. when the follow-up request comes in it can request incremental continuation — the runtime rehydrates the KV and continues. you can also enable automatic retry where the platform requeues continuation requests when capacity frees.
[00:06:18] [00:07:00] Jae: on networking — we have strict egress policies, TLS enforced to corporate proxies, and KMS-based key rotation. if we do Private (VPC) deployment, how do you handle HSM integration?
[00:07:12] Maya: for Private we support customer-managed KMS + HSM via standard KMIP connectors or Cloud KMS. we can run with zero egress if you want fully air-gapped, and we can ship the on-prem package. we also expose audit logs and per-token tracing hooks for compliance.
[00:07:28] Ravi: retention windows on logs — can we limit them to 90 days and redact PII?
[00:07:32] Liam: yes, log retention and redaction rules are configurable per-account. we also have SOC2 docs and a data processing addendum we can share.
[00:07:41] [00:08:00] Maya: quick pause — any concerns we haven't covered so far?
[00:08:05] Simone: one worry — our frontend expects monotonic streaming chunks, and re-ordered partials can break rendering. do you guarantee ordering?
[00:08:12] Liam: ordering is guaranteed per-session. if we do cross-node continuation, we use sequence tokens and reassembly. however, during forced eviction you may see gaps and you'd get the "incomplete" signal. we try to avoid re-ordering.
[00:08:25] [00:09:00] Liam: demo continued — now I'll show a live workload replay. this is an anonymized capture from a previous customer scaled to your traffic. note: transcription sometimes shows product names wrong.
[00:09:12] [00:10:30] Liam: alerting view — you can set latency SLOs and have automatic routing rules that fail open or fail closed. for example when p95 > 350ms we can spike to the dedicated pool. these thresholds are tunable.
[00:10:55] Jae: what's the billing behavior if we use a dedicated pool for 30 minutes during a flash?
[00:11:01] Maya: there are two models: reserved capacity with burst credits, or usage-based with surge pricing. reserved pool gives predictable unit economics; usage-based means you pay for the GPU-hours during the burst. we'll include both in the pilot pricing.
[00:11:14] [00:12:00] Simone: we want to run benchmarks ourselves — are there test harnesses or SDKs we can use to replay our traffic?
[00:12:07] Liam: yes — we provide a perf-harness and a replay tool. we can run a 48-hour synthetic to capture long-tail behavior. we'll also provide a script to generate sequence-length histograms.
[00:12:20] Ravi: what about cold-starts for long models? is there a warm replica strategy?
[00:12:26] Liam: warm replicas for hot models, and prefetching of KV blocks for expected prefixes. for truly huge sessions we recommend a hybrid: summarize old history into embeddings and only keep recent 8k tokens in KV. Optimize will flag sessions that are good candidates for summary compaction.
[00:12:45] [00:13:30] Jae: can you walk through an incident scenario — say a region outage occurs during a flash sale — how would Redwood keep us online?
[00:13:37] Maya: we have multi-region routing and automatic fallback to compatible model variants in another region. you can set a phoenix policy: if primary region latency or capacity crosses threshold, route to another region with optional async replication. during cross-region failover you may see slightly degraded latencies but continuity is maintained.
[00:13:55] [00:15:00] Liam: ok handing over to an example log trace — here's a 503 cascade we saw in synthetic: queue depth spikes, internal shedding policy evicts background scoring, partial responses returned, customers' frontend retried and continued once capacity freed. we instrumented it to surface precise reason codes so you can map alerts to UX.
[00:15:20] Simone: nice. do you provide a debug kit so our SREs can reproduce and triage?
[00:15:25] Liam: yes — we provide trace IDs, a replay package, and local shim to run the same kernel selection path.
[00:15:35] [00:18:00] Maya: security checklist — SOC2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, per-route audit logs, KMS/HSM support, encryption at rest and in transit, network isolation via Private. we'll send the pack.
[00:18:18] Jae: ok good. pricing?
[00:18:21] Maya: I'll send a three-option pilot: 1) Hosted pilot (usage-based), 2) Dedicated reserved pool (monthly commit with burst credits), 3) Private trial (short-term on-prem evaluation). I'll include expected cost delta for enabling the "long-kernel" path and for keeping warm replicas.
[00:18:35] [00:25:00] (demo continues — Liam shows more console screens, Optimize suggestions, and a sample telemetry export. Conversation includes intermittent cross-talk and brief side-chats about internal roadmaps.)
[00:25:12] Simone: small nit — the console exported a CSV and some column names were truncated ("svc_lat_p9" etc). we'll need a clean mapping doc.
[00:25:22] Liam: noted, will include mapping.
[00:30:00] Jae: for the pilot we want to measure three KPIs: 1) p95 token latency under burst, 2) cost per 1k tokens with Optimize enabled, 3) recovery time during simulated region failover.
[00:30:12] Maya: agreed. we'll propose a pilot plan that measures those.
[00:40:00] (technical deep dive between Simone and Liam — sequence-length handling details, quantization tradeoffs, and batch window tuning. transcription picks up filler words and occasional mis-hears: "q5 should be q-5?" becomes "cue five should be cue five" etc.)
[00:50:00] Ravi: operational question — do you provide a service-level credit if p99 latency exceeds X?
[00:50:07] Maya: SLA credits are part of enterprise agreements for Dedicated and Private. Hosted has best-effort SLAs but we can discuss committed SLOs for reserved contracts.
[00:51:30] Simone: last quick question — what telemetry granularity do we get? per-token? per-chunk?
[00:51:37] Liam: telemetry is per-request with token-level breakdowns in the trace export. sampling applies at high TPS to control volume, but you can request increased retention for the pilot.
[00:52:00] [00:60:00] (wrapping up)
[00:60:10] Maya: ok recap — action items: Maya sends pilot pricing; Liam shares console clip and mapping doc; Polaris provides anonymized workload. we'll schedule a pilot kickoff week of 6/23. any objections?
[00:60:28] Jae: no objections. sounds good.
[00:60:35] Simone: thanks, appreciate the pragmatic fallback options.
[00:60:40] Ravi: thanks all.
[00:61:00] Maya: one last note — we'll run a short whiteboarding session with your SREs to configure shedding policies that match your UX priorities.
[00:61:12] Jae: let's do that.
[00:71:30] (call ends)
